newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambia sees 40 percent drop in 1997 maize crop.
newsitem.headline: Zambia sees 40 percent drop in 1997 maize crop.

text.p: Zambia's National Union of Farmers said on Monday that it expected the country's maize crop to drop by around 40 percent this year due to a fertiliser shortage caused by a government liquidity crisis in 1996.

"Due to the late delivery of fertiliser and the inability of farmers to use expensive credit fertiliser, the maize yield is expected to drop by 40 percent to around nine and 10 million 90-kg bags," farmers union chief Ajay Vashee told Reuters.
Zambia produced 15 million 90-kg bags of maize last year, against a national requirement of 12 million.
Vashee said there was now enough fertiliser in the country, but it had arrived too late to be of much use to farmers.
The farmers' union estimated that there were 150,000 tonnes of fertiliser in the country, against a requirement of 110,000 tonnes.
The estimate differs markedly from the government, which puts the total fertiliser requirement at 225,000 tonnes.
"The government does not seem inclined to bring in the shortfall of 114,500 tonnes going by their figures because of cash problems," Vashee said.
Last week, agriculture permanent secretary Austin Sichinga the government would only provide fertiliser for around 90,000 of an estimated 600,000 small scale farmers in the country.

Sichinga said fertiliser imports were delayed because South African suppliers withheld supplies until the government had settled debts of $10 million for 30,000 tonnes of fertiliserr procured in 1995.
The government was supposed to have made the payments in March last year but only managed to do so in October.

Western governments, led by the United States, froze funding to aid-reliant Zambia last year in protest against constitutional changes by President Frederick Chiluba aimed at giving his Movement for Multiparty Democracy advantage in a November 18 general election.
Seven opposition parties boycotted the polls, won by Chiluba in a landslide.
Sichinga said the government had now ordered 49,000 tonnes of fertiliser from South Africa at $26 million.
He said the late arrival of the fertiliser was likely to have an adverse impact on yields.
